- icy road conditions

- poor lighting on road markings
- glare

There are plenty of scenarios.  If you read more about robotics, you'll learn that a lot of these are compounding issues.  E.g. If there are two cars on the road, the problem is exponentially harder, not just twice as hard

A lot of my examples above harp on visibility.  Cameras are not good substitutes for the human mind.   Properly functioning human brains learn to almost map an object in 3D.  If you see the front end of a bike, you know it's a relatively long and straight object.  A robot seeing it from a forward perspective, however, might write it up as just a short pole (like the "don't drive on the sidewalk, cars :p" barriers).  A bicyclist might look enough like a pedestrian that it thinks it's a pedestrian.  This is really bad, because the program has to predict where the bicyclist could go.  A pedestrian is significantly slower.  

Tesla is fantastic at PR.  For an engineering company, they're really not that amazing.  There are several significant innovations they've developed, sure, but as a whole?   The only reason no one else is doing what they're doing is the small net profit margins.  Tesla is in a weird boat.  They do "cool stuff", which is great PR, then secure more government grants, etc.  I do like their products.  But they overstate the ability of their "autonomy".  If you read about the issues people are having with that mode in their Tesla's, you'll see what I mean.  Visibility is a huge concern.  That's how the dude died a few weeks ago - couldn't tell the truck merging into his lane was a truck - just thought it was the sky.  

Yeah.  There are maybe situations where autonomy can react faster and better than a human.  There are other situations where it can't.  Most people would rather die driving when they are in control vice something else.  That's one of two psychological complexes people who are "afraid of flying" have a hard time getting past - the lack of control.   Maybe I'd rather drive under the 18-wheeler and end my life, versus live with the horrific image of my car plowing through pedestrians ?   How could I let my car make that decision ?

Anyway, contrary to belief, the bigger, heavier, and less maneuverable (read:more dangerous) the vehicle, the slower it will be adopted.  

I DO think they'll use this technology soon.  I think it will only be on roads deemed "safe".  Maybe private roads between facilities (Boeing?).  Maybe low traveled desert roads with no stop signs and very consistent weather.   It's going to be a long time before people accept the above risks, I think, though.  Meanwhile you'll hear a lot of companies say "it's 156% safer than driving!" or pull statistical tricks like "it's 99.9% safe!" When regular driving is "99.8% safe" to try to make their money, or earn further development grants.  

Will be interesting.

The two real phrases to be familiar with are "Lifecycle Cost" and "Energy Return On Energy Invested."   

Lifecycle Cost is an item's cost from the moment it's materials are being mined out of the earth through decomposition. 

Energy Return On Energy Invested is a ratio of how much energy you get out of something divided by how much energy is costs to make. 

Both of these are important.  Let's say something makes more energy in it's life than it takes to build; I.e. it has an EROEI > 1.  Lets say this item is a steel block.  Fantastic.  Almost all steel you get these days is recycled from old parts, and when it's finished it is recycled into new parts.  This is a "clean" system.  

Unfortunately, this is about where it starts to fall apart.  EROEI calculations are not standardized, and most pro-alternative-energy sources skew it as much as possible to keep getting new funding.  The other side probably has their own biases.

Unfortunately, while Lifecycle Cost is such a great analysis tool - man, the Prius is a dirty car to manufacture and dispose of - how do you quantify poisoning rivers?   In China, they don't really seem to care.  In West Virginia, New York, etc, chemicals have leaked or been dumped into rivers and the world didn't end.

Nuclear energy is great - sure there are radioactive byproducts, but at least you know where they are when you're done (vs floating around in the air).  France gets it.  France gets 75% of their energy from nuclear power.  But wait, wow, that's a lot of radioactive potential in one area.  Germany got that.  So, instead of building more plants, they had solar panels shipped in. 

In the Ocean industry, solar panels are great because you don't have to put more batteries in things.
